primitives.name: Player Kernel Gaussian Process
primitives.verbatim_quote: - Player kernel: lineup vector z ∈ R^P with z_p = +1 (winner's lineup), -1 (loser's), 0 else; k(z,z′) = σ2z^Tz′.
primitives.assumptions: Players contribute additively to team strength; lineups are static at match start.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Zero covariance for disjoint lineups; singular when all players differ.

layer2.mapping: Maps team outcomes to latent player skill space via inner product of lineup vectors, enabling GP classification without explicit skill parameters.
layer2.telemetry: Log-loss improvement over Elo on national-team tournaments.

reasoning_traces.think:
The core insight is that team strength can be modeled implicitly through shared player contributions using a Gaussian process (GP) framework. The player kernel k(z,z′)=σ²z^Tz′ encodes how much two lineups overlap, enabling the GP to generalize across matches with shared personnel. This is mathematically equivalent to a linear model with one skill per player, but avoids direct estimation of these skills by working in match space. The Zermelo-Bradley-Terry formulation provides a probabilistic interpretation of team strength differences, which aligns with GP classification. The key advantage lies in scalability and robustness to sparse data, especially in domains like soccer with infrequent matches and evolving rosters. In NFL contexts, this allows early-season or backup-QB games to leverage knowledge from other games involving the same players, improving prediction accuracy and uncertainty quantification. Failure modes include overfitting due to small sample sizes or misalignment between club and national-team player pools.
